mqlite HTTP API reference

The broker speaks Connect-style JSON over HTTP. Every operation is a single POST to /mqlite.v1.<Service>/<Method> with a JSON body — curl-able by construction. This document is generated from the wire contract in wire/wire.go (the single source of truth shared by the broker and the Go SDK, so the two can't drift) and the server's error mapping.

This reference describes v0.4.1, the latest supported release. v0.3.3 is withdrawn and unsupported; use the documentation in the v0.3.2 tag when working with its smaller management surface.

Every RPC body must be exactly one non-null JSON object, including operations whose request is otherwise empty ({}). Unknown fields and data after that object are rejected. Repeated fields retain Go's encoding/json behavior: later scalar values replace earlier ones, while repeated object and map values may merge.

Conventions

  • Transport: HTTP POST, Content-Type: application/json. Discovery and health use open GET endpoints; opt-in metrics uses authenticated GET on the same port.
  • body is base64 in JSON (Go marshals []byte as base64).
  • Timestamps are epoch milliseconds (UTC) integers. Message durations use *_ms; observability durations explicitly named *_seconds retain fractional seconds.
  • Sequence numbers (seq_number) are broker-assigned integers, strictly increasing and never reused (they may gap) — the handle you settle with, valid only while the message lives. You never set them.
  • Delivery mode: default Peek-Lock delivery is at-least-once and may repeat, so consumers must be idempotent. Receive-and-delete is an explicit at-most-once broker-removal path that removes a message before returning it; an explicit retry with the same receive attempt ID can replay its saved response. Message TTL configured to discard, DLQ retention, forced resource deletion and fixed subscription expiry are explicit removal paths; see retention.md.
  • One settlement verb per outcome — Complete / Abandon / Reject / Defer, no aliases. New effects require the lock_token from Receive and an unexpired lease; exact-request receipt replays are described below.

Size limits

The message body is capped per message, and the whole request body is capped per RPC call (so an unbounded batch can't OOM the broker before per-message checks run). There is no enforced length limit on the string metadata fields (subject, message_id, group_id, correlation_id, reply_to, content_type, properties keys/values) — they are stored as SQLite TEXT; keep them reasonable (they count toward the JSON request you send, not toward the body cap).

limit default knob
body size 1 MiB → 413 message_too_large over it MQLITE_MAX_MESSAGE_BYTES (serve) / Options.MaxMessageBytes (embedded)
request body per RPC call 32 MiB → 413 message_too_large server.MaxBodyBytes (bodies are base64; split very large batches)
max_messages per Receive 256 (max) request field
wait_time_ms long-poll 20000 (max) request field
Peek max 32 default, 1000 max request field
retained subscriptions 10,000 active + deleting MQLITE_MAX_SUBSCRIPTIONS (serve) / Options.MaxSubscriptions or WithMaxSubscriptions (embedded)
filter expr source capped length + AST node count internal (see concepts.md)

The base URL

Every example below is written against $BASE_URL, because the port is the one thing a reader cannot guess — and guessing it wrong is the whole reason the examples say it out loud now.

# Talking to the broker directly. mqlite serves JSON-over-HTTP on TCP 6754 and terminates
# no TLS of its own, so this is plain http. When enabled, /metrics uses the
# same listener; terminate TLS in a reverse proxy when required.
BASE_URL=http://127.0.0.1:6754

# Behind a reverse proxy. Public HTTPS on 443 (which the URL omits, as usual) terminates at
# the proxy, which forwards to the broker's internal http://…:6754.
BASE_URL=https://mq.example.com

6754 is not a second, binary protocol — there is no binary protocol. It is the port the same JSON-over-HTTP API listens on when nothing is proxying for you.

The discovery card's endpoints are route paths, deliberately relative: they resolve against the origin that served the card, so they inherit its scheme, host and port. Fetch the card from $BASE_URL and the paths are usable as-is. The optional metrics field is the same-origin path /metrics when enabled; it is omitted by default. Resolve it against $BASE_URL like the other paths.

Auth

Use one Authorization: Bearer <token> header. The broker accepts configured administrator tokens in MQLITE_TOKENS (comma-separated), plus managed access keys stored in its database. Secure by default: if MQLITE_TOKENS is unset, mqlite serve generates and prints an administrator token at startup. Newly generated tokens always use mqk_ plus 64 lowercase hexadecimal characters: 256 random bits, 68 ASCII characters in total. Existing configured tokens remain valid without changing their format. Token values are case-sensitive.

Set MQLITE_TOKENS=off to explicitly disable auth (loopback by default; a remote bind needs the explicit insecure override). In that mode, the existing queue API remains open and key-management RPCs are forbidden. An embedded Serve without WithTokens has the same explicit auth-off behavior.

With auth enabled, missing, malformed, unknown, expired or revoked credentials return 401 unauthenticated; a valid key without the required permission returns 403 permission_denied. A key-store failure is a server error, never an auth bypass. Bare tokens, other authentication schemes and duplicate Authorization headers are rejected.

Permissions

Permissions apply to all queues and subscriptions in this broker. Use send, listen, both, or manage; manage includes the other two and may issue new administrator keys. This is consumption permission, not a read-only observer: receiving, settling and renewing change message state.

Required permission Operations
send QueueService/Send, Schedule, Cancel
listen QueueService/Receive, ReceiveDeferred, Peek, Stats, Complete, CompleteBatch, Abandon, Reject, Defer, Renew, RenewBatch; AdminService/Subscribe, TestFilter
manage All other AdminService methods, all AuthService methods, and /metrics
configured monitor AdminService/Observe and /metrics only

Both receive modes require listen, including receive-and-delete. Batch and idempotent replay paths use the same permission checks as the original operation. Subscription inventory and deletion require manage; force changes the deletion precondition, not its permission. A fixed TTL is creation-time advance authorization for automatic cleanup and cannot be added to or changed on an existing subscription. The console's administration views require manage. A configured monitor token opens only its observability views. The public static page alone grants no API access.

In v0.3.2 and later, MQLITE_MONITOR_TOKENS configures comma-separated read-only monitoring credentials alongside administrator authentication. The embedded equivalent is WithMonitorTokens. Monitor and administrator credentials must be distinct; configuring monitor tokens with authentication disabled is rejected. Monitor credentials authenticate without querying the key database, so collection failures remain observable. They cannot peek at bodies, receive, send, change configuration or issue keys. They are rotated through configuration and a broker restart, not the managed-key API; monitor is not a managed-key permission. See observability for a ready-to-run monitoring stack.

Configured administrators and managed manage keys have identical operation rights. Configured credentials are checked first: explicitly placing an existing managed token in MQLITE_TOKENS grants it administrator rights independently of its database permissions, expiry or revocation. Remove it from configuration to withdraw that static grant. Database key operations never alter environment configuration.

Observe

Available in v0.3.2 and later; older brokers do not implement this route.

POST /mqlite.v1.AdminService/Observe with {} returns the canonical broker observation used by /metrics, the SDK Observe, CLI observe, MCP observe and console. Requires manage or a configured monitor credential.

Field Meaning
server_time_ms Broker lifecycle clock near response assembly; absent or zero means unavailable, including on an older compatible broker
sampled_at_ms, started_at_ms, backend, version Queue sampling instant, engine lifetime and non-sensitive identity
access Request capability: manage, monitor or anonymous; SDK embedded mode uses embedded
collection Queue collection state, last_success_at_ms, latest queue-gauge refresh duration_seconds, bounded error_code
queue_count, subscription_count, queues Actual retained state counts and age; counts are usable only when collection is available
runtime Schema version, read-probe availability/latency and local footprint availability/bytes; no DSN or path
messages Engine-lifetime {queue,event,count} effects, recorded after confirmed commits
storage Bounded operation outcomes, durations, retries and database connection pool measurements
maintenance, filters Maintenance enablement, results/durations/last success and filter failures
http Request outcomes/full elapsed time, final authentication outcomes and post-auth handler histograms

Successful authentication returns HTTP 200 even if queue collection is unavailable: queues is then null, with an explicit failure code and the last successful collection time. In-memory counters remain available. Never interpret absent queues or unavailable sizes/probes as zero. Authentication itself still fails closed; a managed key may be unusable while its database is unavailable. Pure embedded observations mark the HTTP domain not_applicable.

The observation is sampled over an interval, not a transaction spanning every runtime counter. Its queue gauges share one aggregate SQL read and one engine clock value. Counters reset on engine/process restart; they are not a durable message ledger. Histograms contain cumulative finite buckets and a total count that is also the Prometheus +Inf bucket. The existing handler histogram excludes authentication; whole-request duration includes it and normal Receive long polls. server_time_ms is read separately near response assembly, from the same broker clock used for lifecycle deadlines. It can therefore advance while a cache hit correctly preserves an older sampled_at_ms.

After a queue or subscription is physically deleted, its process-lifetime message effects move to the documented messages[].queue == "" retired aggregate. v0.4.1 corrects the Go decoder and bundled console to accept that special label while still requiring a complete, unique event domain. Its event semantics and schema token are unchanged from v0.4.0; v0.4.1 separately adds the optional, forward-compatible server_time_ms observation field described above.

The shared decoder bounds observations to 32 MiB and rejects incomplete objects, inconsistent availability and malformed histogram data. The complete JSON schema is represented by wire/observability.go and engine/observability.go; metric semantics and compatibility aliases are specified in observability.

curl -fsS "$BASE_URL/mqlite.v1.AdminService/Observe" \
  -H "Authorization: Bearer $MQLITE_TOKEN" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{}'

CreateKey / ListKeys / RevokeKey

These methods are available in v0.3.1 and later; v0.3.0 does not implement them. All paths are /mqlite.v1.AuthService/<Method> and require manage with authentication enabled.

Method Request Response
CreateKey id, name, permissions, optional expires_at_ms {"key": <AccessKey>, "token": "mqk_…"}
ListKeys optional after_id, limit, sort {"keys": [<AccessKey>], "next_after_id": "…"}; cursor omitted at the end
RevokeKey id {"ok": true}; already revoked records succeed again

AccessKey metadata contains id, name, permissions, created_at_ms, expires_at_ms and revoked_at_ms. Zero expiry means no expiry; zero revocation time means not revoked. Expired and revoked records remain visible to managers. Metadata never contains a token or its digest. Lists include only managed keys; limit defaults to 100 and cannot exceed 1000. Omitted or empty sort means id_asc (public ID ascending). Use sort: "created_desc" for newest first: creation time descending, then public ID descending for equal timestamps.

Pass the previous page's next_after_id as after_id, retaining the same sort. For created_desc, the cursor must identify an existing key; an unknown cursor or unsupported sort returns 400 invalid_argument. Revocation and expiry do not remove records or change their position. Return to the first page to see records newer than the current cursor. Pagination is not a snapshot of concurrent inserts. The id_asc mode also accepts a valid ID that is not present, which supports looking up a retained creation ID using its immediate predecessor and limit: 1.

Before creation, generate and retain a public ID: exactly 32 lowercase hexadecimal characters representing 128 random bits. The SDK provides GenerateKeyID(); the CLI generates one if --id is omitted. This ID is separate from the secret and lets you identify a creation whose response was lost. Names are nonempty UTF-8 labels up to 128 bytes without leading/trailing whitespace or NUL. Names need not be unique. permissions accepts send, listen, or manage; any combination containing manage is normalized to ["manage"]. Expiry is epoch milliseconds, either zero or a future instant.

The server generates the secret and stores only its SHA-256 digest. Save the creation response securely: no later operation can recover the same secret. A duplicate ID returns 409 key_conflict rather than producing or revealing a key. Do not automatically retry a creation after an ambiguous response. Reconcile the retained ID, revoke an undelivered key when confirmed, and use a new ID for its replacement. An absent row does not prove that an outstanding request cannot still commit. Never guess which same-named key to revoke.

Revocation rejects subsequent authentication attempts immediately. Requests already authorized, including a long-poll Receive, may finish. Subsequent settlement and renewal still require a valid key. Issued keys are independent: revoking their creator does not revoke them. Change permissions by issuing a replacement key, moving clients, then revoking the old key.

Open endpoints (no auth)

Method Path Returns
GET / JSON discovery card, or the console for an interactive browser (see below)
GET /healthz 200 ok (liveness)
GET /ui Embedded admin console (when enabled — see below) 
curl "$BASE_URL/"                    # what is this? (no auth)
# → {"name":"mqlite","version":"<the broker's version>","description":"...","status":"ok",
#    "auth":"bearer","docs":"https://github.com/mqlitehq/mqlite",
#    "endpoints":["/mqlite.v1.QueueService/Send", ...every RPC route...],
#    "health":"/healthz","ui":"/ui"}
curl "$BASE_URL/healthz"             # ok

An interactive browser that explicitly prefers text/html receives a temporary redirect from / to /ui/ when the embedded console is enabled. Requests with no Accept header, */*, or application/json continue to receive the exact JSON card above; the response varies on Accept. A headless broker (MQLITE_UI=off) always keeps / as JSON. This preserves machine discovery while making direct browser navigation useful.

The card's auth is "bearer" when RPCs require a token or "none" when auth is off, so an agent can branch on it directly. endpoints is the complete list of RPC route paths (it always matches what the broker serves — a pinned contract). health is the relative liveness path. The optional metrics field is "/metrics" when --metrics or MQLITE_METRICS=on enables the exporter on the API port. It is omitted when disabled, and the route returns 404 even with valid credentials. Enabling metrics requires administrator auth; the advertised route still requires a monitor or administrator credential. No separate URL configuration is needed.

/ui serves the embedded admin console (a static single-page app baked into the binary) and is auth-exempt — the page itself loads without a token; its API calls carry one you paste in. It's on by default; set MQLITE_UI=off to run headless, in which case /ui 404s and the card's optional ui field is omitted.

Other endpoints

Method Path Auth Returns
GET /metrics (when enabled) Bearer with manage or configured monitor Prometheus text: mqlite_queue_messages{queue,state} gauges

QueueService

All paths are /mqlite.v1.QueueService/<Method>.

Send

Enqueue one or more messages in one transaction.

  • Request SendRequest: queue (string), messages ([Message]), scheduled_enqueue_time_ms (int, optional), batch-wide ttl_ms (int, optional). Each input Message may instead carry its own ttl_ms; do not combine a positive batch-wide value with positive per-message values.
  • Response SendResponse: seq_numbers ([int]) — one per input message, positional.
  • Dedup: in a multi-message batch, a slot that hits a dedup conflict (same message_id, different body) comes back as 0 (skipped) while the rest commit. A single-message Send instead returns 409 already_exists.

The batch-wide ttl_ms applies to every message and remains the compact form for a uniform batch. Per-message ttl_ms supports a mixed-TTL batch. When no positive batch-wide TTL is present, zero or omission uses the queue default for that item; otherwise it inherits the positive batch-wide value. MQLite v0.4.1 clients use the batch-wide field when every item has the same TTL and the per-message field only when values differ. An older strict broker rejects that newer mixed-TTL shape instead of silently changing the TTLs.

A positive queue default_ttl_ms is both the default and the ceiling: the effective TTL is the smaller positive value of the message/request and queue values; if only one is positive, that value applies; if neither is positive, expiry is unlimited. Negative TTLs and positive values below the wire's 1 ms precision are invalid, as is an effective deadline that cannot fit in epoch milliseconds. At enqueue, expires_at_ms = initial visible_at_ms + effective TTL, so a scheduled Send starts its TTL at its scheduled visibility time rather than when the request is accepted. Later renewal, delayed Abandon, and scheduler activation do not move expires_at_ms. This message TTL is unrelated to AdminService/Subscribe.ttl_ms, which is the fixed lifetime of the subscription resource and its backing queue.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data "{\"queue\":\"orders\",\"messages\":[{\"body\":\"$(printf hi|base64)\"}]}" \
  "$BASE_URL/mqlite.v1.QueueService/Send"

Receive

Peek-Lock (default) or Receive-and-Delete; long-polls up to wait_time_ms. Receive-and-Delete removes the row before returning it and grants no lease: lock_token is empty and locked_until_ms is zero (omitted when empty), including replays with the same receive attempt ID. The SDK exposes a zero LockedUntil time. Every newly granted Receive claim increments delivery_count; replaying a live receive_attempt_id returns the saved claim and does not increment it again.

  • Request ReceiveRequest: queue, max_messages (int, default 1, max 256), wait_time_ms (int, long-poll; max 20000), receive_mode (int: 0 peek-lock, 1 receive-and-delete), receive_attempt_id (string, optional idempotency key — a retry replays the same batch / same lock tokens).
  • Response ReceiveResponse: messages ([Message]) — each carries a lock_token to settle with (peek-lock mode).
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"queue":"orders","max_messages":1,"wait_time_ms":5000}' \
  "$BASE_URL/mqlite.v1.QueueService/Receive"
# → {"messages":[{
#      "seq_number":42,"lock_token":"lt_9f3a…","delivery_count":1,
#      "body":"aGk=","message_id":"order-42","group_id":"cust-7",
#      "enqueued_at_ms":1750000000000,"locked_until_ms":1750000030000
#    }]}
# settle it: POST .../Complete {"queue":"orders","seq_number":42,"lock_token":"lt_9f3a…"}

Complete / Abandon / Reject / Defer / Renew

All take SettleRequest and return SettleResponse { "ok": true }. Settling with an expired or wrong lock_token → 409 lock_lost, unless a live settlement receipt matches the exact request: queue, seq_number, lock_token, operation, and the arguments that change its effect (delay_ms, or Reject's reason/description). This replay rule applies to Complete/Abandon/Reject/Defer; Renew extends a live lease. New settlement and renewal effects require locked_until_ms > now: the exact deadline already counts as expired, even if the background reaper has not run. The broker samples time after local writer admission and afresh for each statement and remote retry. A live exact-request receipt can replay a previously committed settlement after its original lease deadline; it cannot authorize a different request or revive a lease.

Method Extra fields Effect
Complete — delete the message (done)
Abandon delay_ms (int, optional) release the lock without incrementing delivery_count: below max, redeliver after delay_ms (a delayed head keeps holding its group's line on ordered queues); at max, move to the DLQ
Reject dead_letter_reason, dead_letter_description (optional) move to the DLQ
Defer — set aside; retrieve later by seq via ReceiveDeferred
Renew — extend the same live lease without changing state, token, or delivery_count; cannot revive an expired lease

SettleRequest: queue, seq_number, lock_token (+ the extras above).

For a queue or subscription without a fixed expiry, Renew commits locked_until_ms = max(current locked_until_ms, broker_now + lock_duration_ms). It never shortens a lease, and rapid renewals do not stack durations. For a fixed-life subscription, its absolute expiry caps the candidate deadline. Renew before the current deadline; once the lease is expired, Renew fails with 409 lock_lost.

max_delivery_count is evaluated when a locked attempt fails, not when its final ordinary Peek-Lock claim is granted. For example, with a maximum of 10, an ordinary Peek-Lock Receive may return delivery_count=10; that consumer can renew the lease repeatedly and Complete successfully. If it instead Abandons, lets the lease expire, or leaves the lock for startup recovery, the message goes to the DLQ and is not ordinarily claimed an eleventh time. ReceiveDeferred currently differs, as described below.

Defer + ordering. A deferred message keeps its head-of-line position: in a group_fifo/strict_fifo (or otherwise grouped) queue the messages behind it — its group, or the whole queue under strict_fifo — stay blocked until it is retrieved via ReceiveDeferred and settled (other groups proceed). Normal Receive never returns a deferred message, and with no TTL there is no auto-recovery, so recover a lost seq_number via Peek with state=deferred.

Abandon + ordering. With delay_ms > 0 the message parks as scheduled until the backoff lapses and — like a deferred head — holds its head-of-line position on ordered queues: its group (the whole queue under strict_fifo) is not delivered ahead of it. Below max, no delay makes it redeliver immediately; at max, Abandon moves it to the DLQ regardless of delay_ms. Abandon and the scheduler do not increment delivery_count; only the next claim does. Because Cancel is restricted to never-delivered scheduled sends (delivery_count=0), it cannot remove a retry parked here.

Three separate deadlines. A lock lease controls one attempt. Message TTL controls normal-delivery eligibility and can expire while locked; expiry dead-letters the message by default or discards it when queue policy says so. A fixed subscription lifetime controls the entire subscription and caps its locks. Renew changes only the lease; it does not extend message TTL or subscription lifetime.

CompleteBatch

Complete many messages in one round-trip — settle a whole received batch without a Complete-per-message N+1 (the cheap path for draining).

  • Request CompleteBatchRequest: queue, messages ([{seq_number, lock_token}]).
  • Response CompleteBatchResponse: results ([{seq_number, ok}]) — ok=false for a stale/expired lock on that item (not fatal to the batch). Each item is fenced + idempotent exactly like Complete.

RenewBatch

Extend the lock lease of a whole received batch in one round-trip.

Renewing message-by-message costs one request per message, so on a slow link a renewal pass can take longer than the lease it is renewing — a 64-message batch at 50 ms per call needs 3.2 s against a 2 s lock, and most of the locks expire mid-pass.

  • Request RenewBatchRequest: queue, messages ([{seq_number, lock_token}]). At most 512 messages per call — more returns 400 invalid_argument.
  • Response RenewBatchResponse: results ([{seq_number, ok, locked_until_ms}]). ok=false for a stale/expired lock on that item (not fatal to the batch); each item is fenced on its own lock_token, exactly like Renew.

locked_until_ms is the deadline the broker actually committed — renew again before it. And ok=true means the lease was live when the broker's statement finished — not when the answer reaches you. The result still has to be mapped, encoded and travel back, so on a very short lease it can lapse on the way. locked_until_ms is the authoritative fact: compare it against your own clock. (If the write itself outlived the lock, you get ok=false rather than a lock you never really held.) Like single-message Renew, the batch operation leaves token, state, and delivery_count unchanged and commits the later of the existing deadline and the broker's fresh now + lock_duration candidate (capped by a fixed subscription lifetime).

Why 512? Renewal is a claim about the future ("this lease is live"), and that claim is only keepable within a single statement: across several, the first batch's lease can expire — and be reaped — while a later one is still running. Receive hands out at most 256 messages, so a consumer never meets the limit by accident. (CompleteBatch has no such limit, because completion is terminal: it reports what already happened.)

ReceiveDeferred

Lock previously-Defer'd messages by sequence number.

  • Request ReceiveDeferredRequest: queue, seq_numbers ([int]).
  • Response ReceiveResponse: messages ([Message]).
  • Each successful by-sequence claim increments delivery_count. It currently does not reject a deferred message merely because its count is already at max_delivery_count; after retrieval, normal settlement/DLQ rules still apply. Consequently, the ordinary retry path is bounded at its Nth claim, but this explicit recovery path can produce a count above N.

Schedule

Enqueue for future delivery (same wire shape as Send).

  • Request SendRequest with scheduled_enqueue_time_ms set (epoch ms).
  • Response SendResponse: seq_numbers.

Cancel

Delete a scheduled send that has never been delivered (delivery_count=0). A delayed Abandon may also be in scheduled, but it cannot be cancelled.

  • Request CancelRequest: queue, seq_number. Response SettleResponse.

Peek

Browse without locking or settling (triage; recover a deferred seq).

  • Request PeekRequest: queue, from_seq (int, optional), state (string, optional: active/locked/deferred/scheduled/dead_lettered), max (int, default 32, max 1000).
  • Response PeekResponse: messages ([Message], includes state + dead_letter_reason/description).

Stats

  • Request MetricsRequest: queue.
  • Response MetricsResponse: queue, active, locked, deferred, scheduled, dead_lettered, total, oldest_message_age_ms. The age is measured from the oldest active or locked message; it is zero when neither state is present.
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"queue":"orders"}' "$BASE_URL/mqlite.v1.QueueService/Stats"
# → {"queue":"orders","active":128,"locked":3,"deferred":0,"scheduled":5,
#    "dead_lettered":2,"total":138,"oldest_message_age_ms":41200}

AdminService

All paths are /mqlite.v1.AdminService/<Method>.

DeleteQueue

v0.4.0 uses the corrected name-only contract below. The incompatible request shape shipped in the withdrawn, unsupported v0.3.3 release; its public artifacts remain available for forensic or compatibility inspection and must not be deployed. v0.4.0 carries the retract v0.3.3 directive for Go module tools.

Deletes a plain queue. Requires administrator/manage permission. The default is empty-only; force is a separate, explicit authorization to discard retained work.

  • POST /mqlite.v1.AdminService/DeleteQueue
  • Request: {"name":"orders"} or {"name":"orders","force":true}.
  • A completed deletion returns {"deleted":true,"state":"deleted"}. If bounded cleanup remains, acceptance returns {"deleted":false,"state":"deleting"}. Both are successful, authoritative outcomes; any other acknowledgement shape is outcome_unknown to a client.
  • Without force, any retained message row blocks deletion, including active, locked, scheduled, deferred, completed and dead-lettered states: HTTP 409, queue_not_empty. Drain or settle them first. With force, all of those rows are permanently discarded. A locked delivery may already have caused an external side effect; deleting its broker record cannot undo that effect.
  • Subscription backing queues are rejected with HTTP 400, invalid_argument; this operation does not remove topic subscriptions.
  • The accepting transaction changes the queue to deleting and starts bounded cleanup. If cleanup finishes, the same commit removes the queue and returns deleted; otherwise it commits the deleting marker. From that point, queue operations are rejected without taking effect. Name-addressed operations such as Send, Receive, Peek and Stats return not_found; a stale lock settlement may instead report lock_lost. An existing long poll is woken, CreateQueue with that name returns name_conflict, and ListQueues continues to expose the reserved name with state:"deleting". The discard authorization is durable, and background cleanup needs no follow-up delete.
  • One foreground call removes at most 1,000 physical queue-owned rows and targets about 8 MiB. A single larger row is still removed so cleanup can progress. A pending delete wakes a background pass that globally caps cleanup at 4,096 rows and targets about 8 MiB. The ordinary path visits at most 32 loaded resources on a local store or one loaded resource on remote Turso/libSQL, bounding remote round trips inside the write transaction. A separate set-based path can finalize up to 512 empty subscriptions without using that resource-count allowance; its mapping and backing rows still use the shared row budget. A full 512-subscription fast-path batch schedules its next pass after 10 ms. Other required continuation passes are paced one second apart; an idle broker does not poll for lifecycle work. The persisted cursor rotates through pending names fairly on both backends, so a large or bursty deletion cannot monopolize the single writer. Startup resumes one bounded pass before crash recovery. The row and name vanish only after messages, deduplication, settlement receipts and receive-attempt records are gone. Message sequence numbers are not reset, and process event counters remain historical.
  • Missing queues return HTTP 404, not_found. Once a deleting name disappears, this is also the completed state observed by a later reconciliation request.
  • Stop producers and consumers before retiring a queue. The transactional empty-only check prevents deletion of a concurrent acknowledged send. Force deliberately replaces that protection with discard permission.
  • Queue names are reusable, and the public API deliberately has no lifetime token. One owner must serialize deletion and same-name recreation. Wait for a successful state:"deleted" response, or confirm that ListQueues no longer contains a previously deleting name, before creating its replacement. Never replay an old deletion after recreation.
  • The SDK and MCP client each call their configured HTTP transport once and do not follow HTTP redirects. Transport failures, redirects, every HTTP 5xx response (including a gateway-generated response), and invalid successful acknowledgements are outcome_unknown. Configure custom transports and proxies not to retry these destructive routes. Keep the name reserved and inspect ListQueues. Under the single-owner rule, an absent row confirms the deletion; a deleting row means cleanup is still running. Never use another delete as a status check or automatically retry it. The engine performs up to 30 one-second discovery passes after an uncertain remote database commit so a late-visible retirement can enter normal cleanup; startup recovery is the durable fallback. Concurrent delete/recreate controllers are unsupported.
  • When access logging is retained, the operation record includes its server request ID, safe actor classification, queue, force decision, acceptance, and returned lifecycle state. See destructive-operation evidence.

Go SDK: client.DeleteQueue(ctx, name) error and the equivalent embedded method retain their empty-only signature. They return nil once deletion is accepted, including when bounded cleanup continues in the background. Use DeleteQueueWithOptions(ctx, name, mqlite.DeleteQueueOpts{Force: true}) to authorize discard and receive the Deleted / State outcome. Reconcile a deleting or unknown outcome read-only via ListQueues; background cleanup progresses without another delete.

The public identity remains the queue name; force does not introduce a lifetime token. Durable deletion and fixed-lifetime metadata make v0.4.0 schema token 7, which refuses schema-5 and schema-6 files rather than migrating them. Schema 6 belonged only to intermediate unreleased builds and was never tagged. The console exposes delete queue in a plain queue's detail page and requires an exact name confirmation. A nonempty queue additionally requires a force checkbox and shows the locked-delivery side-effect warning. If an accepted deletion is still cleaning up, the console reconciles with ListQueues; it does not issue a second delete that could target a same-name replacement. Older brokers report the operation as unsupported.

DeleteSubscription

Available in v0.4.0.

Deletes one exact topic/subscription pair. It uses the same durable, bounded lifecycle as DeleteQueue, but owns both the topic roster mapping and the subscription's backing queue.

Requires manage for both empty-only and forced deletion. The force field is explicit discard authorization, not a separate permission tier.

  • POST /mqlite.v1.AdminService/DeleteSubscription
  • Request: {"topic":"events","name":"worker"} or the same object with "force":true. A wrong topic for a globally unique subscription name is 404 not_found; it never selects the subscription by name alone.
  • Response: {"deleted":true,"state":"deleted"} or {"deleted":false,"state":"deleting"}. Without force, any retained message state returns 409 subscription_not_empty. Force is the caller's durable authorization to discard all states, including locked deliveries.
  • The accepted transaction marks the backing queue deleting and begins bounded cleanup. If cleanup finishes, the same commit removes the mapping and backing queue and returns deleted; otherwise the committed mapping and name remain available for reconciliation while the subscription is excluded from fan-out and direct queue operations. Retiring the last active subscription therefore makes the implicit topic unavailable for fan-out immediately. A deleting mapping keeps the topic address reserved until physical cleanup completes.
  • The SDK methods are DeleteSubscription (empty-only) and DeleteSubscriptionWithOptions(..., DeleteSubscriptionOpts{Force:true}). The built-in destructive clients call their HTTP transport once and classify redirects, transport failures, every HTTP 5xx, and invalid success bodies as an uncertain outcome. Reconcile that outcome with ListSubscriptionsPage using the same topic and include_deleting:true; do not replay the deletion.
  • Subscription identity is still name-only. One owner must serialize deletion and recreation, and temporary subscription names should be globally unique and used for only one lifetime.
  • Retained access logs record the topic/subscription target, force decision, acceptance and returned lifecycle state without storing a Bearer token. See destructive-operation evidence.

CreateQueue

Create a queue, or update one (idempotent upsert on name: calling it again with the same name and the same kind overwrites that queue's config — existing messages are untouched). Names are one flat namespace shared with subscriptions and topics: a name that is live as a topic, or that belongs to an entity of a different kind (e.g. a plain create over a subscription's backing queue), is rejected with 409 name_conflict instead of silently taking over (concepts → provisioning). Response {} (Empty).

Request CreateQueueRequest: name (valid UTF-8, 1–128 bytes) + config (QueueConfigJSON, all fields optional — omit one to take its default). Every duration is epoch milliseconds. Config is queue-level: it's set here, not per Send/Receive.

Field Type Default Meaning
kind string queue queue (normal). subscription can reconfigure an existing legitimate backing queue through the advanced engine/wire surface, but cannot create a backing queue without a topic mapping; use Subscribe to create one.
lock_duration_ms int (ms) 30000 (30s) the peek-lock window. At locked_until_ms, new settlement and renewal fail immediately; the reaper later returns the row to active below the delivery limit or dead-letters it at the limit. Renew uses this duration to extend the same live attempt; the committed deadline is never earlier than the existing one. There is no per-Receive override — it's fixed by the queue. 0 → the 30s default.
max_delivery_count int 10 ordinary delivery-attempt budget. The Nth ordinary Peek-Lock Receive is a usable final attempt; it is dead-lettered with reason=MaxDeliveryCountExceeded only if that locked attempt is abandoned, its lease expires, or it is recovered on startup at delivery_count >= N. ReceiveDeferred increments the count but currently does not use N as an admission check. 0 → the default of 10.
default_ttl_ms int (ms) 0 = unlimited default and ceiling for message TTL. A shorter positive Send ttl_ms is honored; a longer one is capped. For a scheduled Send the effective TTL starts at scheduled visibility. On expiry normal delivery ends and the message goes to the DLQ or is discarded — see dead_letter_on_expire.
dead_letter_on_expire bool true on TTL expiry: true → move to the DLQ; false → discard silently.
dedup_window_ms int (ms) 0 = off duplicate-detection window. 0 disables dedup entirely (then message_id is just metadata). >0 collapses repeats of the same message_id within the window — see The Message object → message_id, dedup & uniqueness.
ordering_mode string standard standard (per-GroupID FIFO, cross-group parallel; ungrouped messages unordered) · group_fifo (same, but every send must carry a group_id → else 400 group_required) · strict_fifo (one global head-of-line FIFO for the whole queue). See conformance §5.
dlq_max_age_ms int (ms) 0 = inherit per-queue DLQ retention override: drop dead letters older than this. 0 inherits the broker default, -1 = unbounded. See retention.md.
dlq_max_count int 0 = inherit keep at most N dead letters (oldest dropped first). 0 inherits, -1 = unbounded.
dlq_max_bytes int 0 = inherit cap total dead-letter body bytes. 0 inherits, -1 = unbounded.

The DLQ values configure asynchronous retention targets. They do not reject new dead letters or synchronously enforce a hard cap, so a queue may temporarily exceed them between worker passes or while bounded cleanup catches up.

curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"name":"orders","config":{
            "lock_duration_ms":60000,
            "max_delivery_count":5,
            "dedup_window_ms":300000,
            "ordering_mode":"group_fifo"
          }}' \
  "$BASE_URL/mqlite.v1.AdminService/CreateQueue"
# → {}

Subscribe

Register subscription name under topic (creates its backing queue). Requires listen; manage includes listen.

This is a broker-wide upsert, not create-only ownership. A listener that knows an existing (topic,name) can update its filter, and a new permanent or temporary subscription consumes the shared capacity and adds publish fan-out. Subscription inventory and explicit deletion remain manage operations. Listen-only clients should set a fixed TTL on temporary subscriptions and leave early retirement to a manager.

  • Request SubscribeRequest: topic, name, filter (optional — {"expr": "<predicate>"}, an expr boolean over the message; empty/omitted matches all). Topic and subscription names are valid UTF-8 strings of 1–128 bytes. A malformed expr or name is rejected with 400 invalid_argument. Response {}.
  • The same route accepts SubscribeWithOptionsRequest, which adds optional ttl_ms in v0.4.0. A positive integer stores a fixed lifetime from the first successful creation; omitted or zero creates a permanent subscription when the name is new, and preserves an existing subscription's lifetime. JSON null, fractions, strings, negative values and integer overflow, plus Go SDK durations between zero and one millisecond, return 400 invalid_argument. The Go methods are Subscribe and SubscribeWithOptions(..., SubscribeOptions{TTL: 15*time.Minute}); the legacy request struct and method are unchanged.
  • Re-subscribing the same (topic,name) with TTL omitted or zero preserves the original deadline while allowing a filter update. Repeating its original positive TTL is idempotent and also does not extend the deadline. A different positive TTL, including an attempt to turn a permanent subscription into a temporary one, returns 409 name_conflict before the filter changes. A temporary subscription cannot be made permanent in place; delete it and create a new lifetime.
  • At now >= expires_at_ms the subscription immediately leaves topic fan-out and every backing-queue operation. Expiry is preauthorization for forced bounded cleanup, including retained messages. The name remains reserved until physical cleanup completes. This guarantee does not undo external effects already caused by a locked delivery. Creation and enforcement use the broker host's UTC clock; keep that clock synchronized because a forward step can expire a subscription early and a backward step can delay a deadline that has not yet been durably transitioned to deleting.
  • The bundled console limits entered TTLs to 3,650 fixed 24-hour days so their millisecond value remains exact in browser JavaScript. Direct HTTP and Go SDK clients retain the API's wider checked-integer range.
  • Name conflicts are rejected with 409 name_conflict: a topic that names an existing queue or subscription, a name that belongs to a plain queue / another topic's subscription / a live topic, and topic == name. Re-subscribing the same (topic, name) is the idempotent filter-update path and succeeds.
  • Active and deleting subscriptions share a configurable global capacity. The default is 10,000. Creating a new mapping at capacity returns 429 resource_exhausted; updating the filter of an existing active mapping is still allowed. A deleting mapping releases its slot only after bounded physical cleanup completes.
  • A database created by an older build may contain a kind=subscription backing queue with no topic mapping. When capacity is available, repair it by calling Subscribe for the intended topic/name, then use DeleteSubscription if the orphan should be retired. Do not edit MQLite-owned tables directly.
curl -H "Authorization: Bearer $T" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  --data '{"topic":"replies","name":"request-01J...","ttl_ms":900000}' \
  "$BASE_URL/mqlite.v1.AdminService/Subscribe"
# → {}

ListQueues

The state field and deleting-resource visibility below are available in v0.4.0.

  • Request {}. Response ListQueuesResponse: queues ([{name, kind, state, lock_duration_ms, max_delivery_count, default_ttl_ms, dedup_window_ms}]). state is active or deleting. Deleting queues remain listed while their name is reserved, but their data plane is unavailable. A fixed-lifetime subscription is reported as deleting at its deadline even if the periodic transition has not yet persisted the state; the legacy fields do not expose its deadline.

ListSubscriptions

  • Requires manage because the result inventories broker-wide names and filters.
  • Request {}. Response {subscriptions: [{topic, name, expr}]} — every active subscription with its topic and filter expression (expr empty = match all). This compatibility-only route is active/unexpired-only and intentionally not paged. It is deprecated for management and reconciliation because it cannot expose deleting name reservations. The configured subscription ceiling bounds its maximum size; new integrations should use the paged route below. The Go SDK retains the original three-field SubscriptionInfo type for this method.

ListSubscriptionsPage

Available in v0.4.0.

  • Requires manage, including when it is used to reconcile deletion or expiry.
  • POST /mqlite.v1.AdminService/ListSubscriptionsPage.
  • Request fields: topic (optional exact topic), after (an opaque cursor from the previous response), limit (0 or omitted = 100, maximum 1,000), and include_deleting (default false).
  • Response: {"subscriptions":[{"topic","name","expr","state","created_at_ms","expires_at_ms"}],"total":N,"next_after":"..."}. state is active or deleting; next_after is omitted on the final page. Both timestamps are required epoch-millisecond integers. expires_at_ms=0 means permanent; otherwise it is greater than created_at_ms and never moves. An expired row is reported as deleting immediately, even before the periodic transition has persisted that state. The default view excludes such rows; include_deleting=true includes them for reconciliation. total counts the complete selected scope at the snapshot used for that request and is independent of after/limit. Go page entries use SubscriptionPageItem, whose required State field is separate from the legacy SubscriptionInfo type.
  • Ordering is (topic,name) and pagination is keyset-based. Cursors are opaque and bound to topic plus include_deleting; reusing one with a different scope returns 400 invalid_argument. limit may change between pages.
  • Each request is internally consistent. A sequence of requests is not a frozen database snapshot, so concurrent creates and deletes can change later pages and their total. Consumers that need a stable administrative export should quiesce subscription changes for the traversal.
  • The Go SDK and MCP tool reject a successful page that is null, incomplete, oversized, out of order, outside the requested topic/state scope, or inconsistent with its total, page size, or cursor progress. Such a response is not valid evidence for destructive-operation reconciliation.

TestFilter

  • Requires listen; it evaluates only the caller-provided expression and sample and does not read or mutate broker data.
  • Request {expr, message?} — dry-run a filter expression: it compiles expr and, if message (a sample, body base64) is given, evaluates it exactly as publish-time fan-out would (nothing is enqueued).
  • Response {valid, error?, ran, matched} — valid = compiled; error = the precise compile error or a runtime/eval error; ran = a sample was evaluated; matched = the sample would route to a subscription using this filter.

Redrive

Move dead-lettered messages back to active (or to another queue). Each internal batch is atomic: a same-queue state change commits as one unit, and a cross-queue source deletion commits with its target insertion. With rate_per_sec, each throttled chunk is a separate atomic batch. Later delivery to a consumer remains at-least-once, so handlers and external effects must remain idempotent.

  • Request RedriveRequest: queue, target (string, optional — cross-queue), max (int), older_than_ms (int), rate_per_sec (int). Response RedriveResponse: moved (int).

Purge

Permanently delete dead-lettered messages.

  • Request PurgeRequest: queue, max (int), older_than_ms (int; both zero purges the whole DLQ). Response PurgeResponse: purged (int). Retained access logs include both requested bounds and the confirmed purge count; see destructive-operation evidence.

Status

A desensitized runtime snapshot for an ops view — never includes a connection string or auth token.

  • Request {}. Response StatusResponse: version, backend (memory | local file | remote libSQL/Turso), remote (bool), location (a local path, or a masked remote host like libsql://***.turso.io), schema_version, ping_ms (a SELECT 1 read round-trip; -1 if it failed), db_size_bytes (local on-disk footprint: db + WAL + shm; 0 for memory/remote), queues, subscriptions, server_time_ms (UTC epoch milliseconds from the broker clock used for lifecycle deadlines), uptime_ms, auth (bool). An absent or zero server_time_ms means the clock is unavailable, including when a current client connects to an older broker that omitted it.

The Message object

One shape for both send input and receive/peek output (fields are omitted when empty). "Dir" = whether you set it on send (in) or the broker sets it on receive/peek (out).

Field Type Dir Meaning · constraints
body base64 in the payload, opaque to the broker (it never parses it). The only size-capped field — ≤ 1 MiB by default (413 over it). Empty body is allowed.
message_id string in optional dedup / idempotency key. No effect unless the queue has dedup on (dedup_window_ms > 0); empty → the body's SHA-256 is used. Not required to be unique. See the next section.
group_id string in ordering / session key — messages with the same group_id are FIFO among themselves (= SQS MessageGroupId / ASB SessionId). Required on every send to a group_fifo queue (else 400 group_required); strict_fifo is one global FIFO and does not need a group_id. Not a consumer group.
subject string in free-form routing label (= ASB Label). Not unique, may repeat or be empty. Split on . into subject_parts for filters ("orders.eu.new" → ["orders","eu","new"]).
correlation_id, reply_to, content_type string in free-form ASB-style metadata; the broker stores but never interprets them (content_type only hints filter body_json decoding).
properties object<string,string> in custom string→string headers, stored verbatim; visible to filters as properties["k"]. Values must be strings.
ttl_ms int (ms) in optional per-message TTL for mixed-TTL batch Send; without a positive batch-wide TTL, zero/omitted uses the queue default. A positive value must be at least 1 ms and is mutually exclusive with a positive batch-wide SendRequest.ttl_ms; all effective TTLs are still capped by a positive queue default.
seq_number int out broker-assigned, strictly increasing, never reused (may gap); the handle you settle/peek with while the message lives.
delivery_count int out how many Receive / ReceiveDeferred claims have been granted. Settlement, renewal, and scheduled activation do not increment it.
lock_token string out fencing token from peek-lock Receive; settle with it.
state string out Peek only: active/locked/deferred/scheduled/dead_lettered.
enqueued_at_ms, expires_at_ms, visible_at_ms, locked_until_ms int out epoch-ms timestamps.
dead_letter_reason, dead_letter_description string out populated for DLQ messages.

message_id, dedup & uniqueness

The single most-asked question: can the sender set message_id, and what happens on a collision?

  • Yes, the sender sets it (it's an optional input field). It is not required to be unique, and the broker assigns nothing here — leave it empty and the field just stays empty (the dedup path, if active, falls back to the body's SHA-256).
  • What the broker does with it depends entirely on the queue's dedup_window_ms:
queue dedup effect of message_id
off (dedup_window_ms = 0, the default) purely informational metadata. No uniqueness is enforced and a collision is impossible — send the same message_id a thousand times and you get a thousand independent messages (each its own seq_number). Use it as an idempotency hint your own consumer checks.
on (dedup_window_ms > 0) within the sliding window, keyed by (queue, message_id):
• same id + same body → collapses to one enqueue (the duplicate is silently dropped; you get the original seq_number back).
• same id + different body → a conflict: a single Send returns 409 already_exists (ErrDedupConflict); in a multi-message Send that one slot comes back as seq 0 (skipped) while the rest commit.
• empty id → the body's SHA-256 is the key (content-addressed dedup).
  • Dedup is per-queue. The key is (queue, message_id), so the same message_id in two different queues — or fanned out to two subscriptions' backing queues — never collides; each is independent.
  • So "can self-specifying cause a problem?" Only if (a) the queue has dedup on and (b) you reuse an id within the window with a different body — that's the deliberate conflict signal. With dedup off (default), or with identical bodies, there is no problem.

Errors

Errors are a JSON envelope {"code": "...", "message": "..."} with an HTTP status:

HTTP code When
400 invalid_argument malformed JSON, a non-object or null request body, an unknown field, trailing data after the object, a bad filter expression, an empty queue name, or an unknown enum (kind / ordering_mode). The decoder is strict — a typo'd field is a 400, not a silently-dropped no-op (mqlite.ErrInvalidArgument).
400 group_required a group_fifo send with no group_id
401 unauthenticated missing/invalid Bearer token (auth is on by default; only MQLITE_TOKENS=off disables it)
403 permission_denied a valid key lacks permission, or key management was attempted with auth disabled (mqlite.ErrPermissionDenied)
404 not_found the queue, exact topic/subscription pair, or message doesn't exist; or an unknown path
409 already_exists single-message dedup conflict (same id, different body)
409 name_conflict a queue/subscription/topic name collision at creation time, including a name reserved by a deleting queue — the namespace is one and disjoint (Subscribe/CreateQueue)
409 key_conflict a managed key ID or token digest is already registered (mqlite.ErrKeyConflict); no existing secret is returned
409 lock_lost settle with an expired or wrong lock_token
409 queue_not_empty deletion found retained messages in at least one state
409 subscription_not_empty subscription deletion found retained messages in at least one state
429 resource_exhausted the active plus deleting subscription capacity is full (mqlite.ErrSubscriptionLimit)
413 message_too_large a message body over MaxMessageBytes (default 1 MiB), or request decoding that exceeds server.MaxBodyBytes (default 32 MiB)
499 canceled the client canceled the request
503 outcome_unknown a remote (Turso/libSQL) write lost its commit acknowledgement — it may or may not have applied. Do not blindly retry; reconcile messages by message_id/dedup, or key operations by their retained public key ID (mqlite.ErrOutcomeUnknown). Only occurs against a remote store, never a local file/:memory:.
500 internal unexpected server error

The 503 outcome_unknown row describes a response generated by the broker. The Go SDK treats every HTTP 5xx received for a lifecycle delete as ErrOutcomeUnknown, even when its envelope says internal, because an intermediary may have generated that response after the broker committed.

The Go SDK re-exports sentinel errors such as mqlite.ErrLockLost, ErrDedupConflict, ErrInvalidArgument and ErrOutcomeUnknown, so errors.Is works in both embedded and client mode. An accepted queue or subscription deletion is a successful operation even when its typed HTTP result is state:"deleting".
